subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews). Has any decision been handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada with respect to the tariff board jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend's question I may say that we received notice this forenoon that judgment has been given on the question submitted. I have not yet received copies of the judgment, but I have before me a memorandum showing the answers returned by the supreme court to the questions submitted. They are as follows:
1.	Has the tariff board as constituted under chapter 7 of the statutes of 1932-33 authority to determine questions of law as distinct from questions of fact?
No.
2.	Has the tariff board authority under said act to determine that the orders of the Minister of National Revenue aforesaid, fixing the values for duty of such goods, under the authority of section 43 of the Customs Act as enacted by chapter 2 of the statutes of 1930 (second session), prior to the enactment of chapter 7 of the statutes of 1932-33, were annulled' and ceased to be effective from the

Tariff Board
date of the last mentioned enactment in respect of goods entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff?
No.
3.	When the tariff board acts under the provisions of part II of the said act, are its decisions as to the value of goods for duty purposes subject to the approval of the Minister of National Revenue?
Yes.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Leader of the Opposition): In view of the answers just read by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) to the questions submitted to the supreme court might I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) if it is the intention of the government at this session to bring in legislation which will help to ensure that the representations made at the time the Ottawa agreements were passed will be given due effect. As I read the answers, they would appear to run counter to what at the time was stated to be the intention of the government with respect to at least one of the purposes of the tariff board.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they are not. The
decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada are wholly in accordance with the representations and statements made at the time the Ottawa agreements were concluded.
I am glad to avail myself of this opportunity to clear up misrepresentations-I trust they were not deliberate-with respect to the meaning of the Tariff Board Act, When the statute was before this house I stated and restated that this was to be a fact finding body. No member of this house has any doubt about that; if he has he can consult Hansard. The supreme court has decided that the board had no power to determine questions of law, but only questions of fact. I have never been able to understand just why any other view was entertained. The second question was, "Has the tariff board authority under the said act to determine that the orders of the minister made under the old statute were not binding" and the court held that the statute we passed rescinding section 43 in its operations, as promised, did not operate with respect to orders made before that statute was passed. That is all. I resent even the suggestion that every promise made has not been implemented to the full with respect to those agreements. The promise was that at the earliest possible date consistent with financial conditions we would rescind the power conferred upon the minister to fix the value for duty purposes of goods coming from Great Britain. In 1932-33, by chapter 7 of the statutes of that year, we did pass an act that had the effect of making it no longer possible for the Minister of National Revenue, under section 43, So fix the value for duty purposes on goods imported from Great Britain. There is no power now in the minister to fix the value under section 43 of goods imported from Great Britain; the statute rescinding and destroying that power as it formerly existed was enacted by this house and the Senate and given the royal assent. But there were outstanding two or three orders fixing values, and the tariff board decided that those orders were invalid although they had been passed prior to the date of the amending statute that removed from the minister the power to fix values. The supreme court has decided that those orders were not thus made invalid. That is that.
It is a little difficult to understand why there was any doubt as to the next question. It was merely that the statute provided under part 2, which substitutes the tariff board for the old customs board so that they may not sit in judgment upon themselves, that the same power that was possessed by the customs board should be retained, and that power is still retained by reason of the anstver given to the third question. In other words, unless the statute is repealed or amended by parliament it does not by implication, through the creation of a new board instead of the customs board, result in the amendment or repeal of that section of the statute.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister if the impression to whioh he refers was not held pretty generally in England? If I am not mistaken the impression in Great Britain was due largely to remarks made by Lord Hailsham with respect to his understanding of the functions of the tariff board in protecting British exporters and the rights secured to them under the agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext:
I have no right to enter into a debate on this matter, Mr. Speaker, but I have seen no statement made by Lord Hailsham that is at variance with what was decided by the supreme court. I do not think for a single moment that he had any idea that there was any doubt as to the fact that this was a fact finding body and not a court of law to decide questions of law, that the customs board had really divested itself of its jurisdiction by statute, and the jurisdiction that it formerly had was thereby * vested in the tariff board. I am not unmindful of the fact that many misrepresentations have arisen in England with respect to the tariff board and other matters, but I am also aware of the source from which such misinformation was disseminated.
Special War Revenue Act

subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: May I ask if the decision of the supreme court was unanimous?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: I cannot answer that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: Yes, I understand that it was unanimous.

subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: Of course we cannot discuss this matter now, and it is not my purpose to defend the views of the distinguished chairman of the tariff board, who no doubt will avail himself of t'he lecture he received to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: I have not lectured him. I resent that.

subtopic: DECISION OF SUPREME COURT AS TO RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: My right hon. friend has plainly stated that he cannot understand why there has been any doubt held by anyone as to this interpretation. The chairman of the tariff board held a different view of the matter from that entertained by my right hon. friend.

Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 97, to amend the Special War Revenue Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 1-Stamp tax on postal notes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Finance if the bill is based in its entirety on the resolutions which were very fully discussed when the house was in committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This bill deals only with the resolutions which have been passed, arising out of the budget, with the exception of one or two changes which deal entirely with administrative matters. There is no change in substance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If there are any new features would the minister direct our attention to them, and in that way possibly save some time.
May I ask the Minister of Finance for an answer to the question I raised about affixing stamps to money orders. Is it necessary to affix the 6tamp or to have the stamp printed on the comer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, upon inquiry I have found that this wording is precisely the same as has obtained hitherto. The word "affixing" does not mean that there must be an actual physical addition of a stamp upon a document, but that the printing or embossing covers the ward "affixing."

If it were embossed I would not object, but it is not embossed. However, my reason for asking the question was that I wanted to clear up the matter as to the question of revenue between the Post Office Department and the Department of National Revenue, so that we would be able to distinguish the amount of work done by the Post Office Department entitling it to that revenue. I say now that they are doing no work, and that the revenue should be credited directly to the Department of National Revenue. The printing on the corner of post office orders, money orders or postal notes is not done by the Post Office Department. It is paid for outside the department, and therefore that department does nothing to earn that amount of money. It should be credited to the proper department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take no exception to what the hon. member for Gloucester has said. In fact, he might go a little farther and deal also with the question of the use of postage stamps, instead of excise stamps, which run into a very considerable volume of money, and he would portray a picture which is. not accurate with respect to the revenue of the Post Office Department. However that is a larger question which will have to be dealt with later.
It is a false picture.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.

On section 3-Excise tax on unstamped packages of cigarette paper or cigarette paper tubes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Section,? 4 to 10 inclusive agreed to.
On section 11-Drawback.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a new section, but dealing with a purely administrative matter. It is to broaden the payment of drawback on goods exported, and to assist Canadian manufacturers in competition on the world's market. The reason for not exempting fuel is that this is used in the plants to supply heat and power, and it is almost impossible to allocate the division of fuel, first, as between heat and power and, secondly, as between domestic and exported goods. It is thought that to make a provision for drawback in respect to excise tax would meet with considerable controversy as to the correct proportion, and it would be difficult if not impossible to administer. This is a broadening of the item.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 12-Additional penalties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is new. The only change in this instance is to make it clear that a penalty may be applied to a taxpayer in addition to the interest on outstanding arrears. It has been a question in some quarters whether when such interest is called a penalty a taxpayer who is delinquent in payment may be required to pay any other penalty for default than the interest, and the present section is designed to clarify the point.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-Officer may make inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is also administrative. At the present time there is no authority provided in the act for the examination of certain businesses. In order to ensure that the taxes imposed by the act were being properly paid, while there has been no opposition made as to the inquiry upon the part of the department, it is thought wise to have a legislative provision so as to prevent any difficulty arising in the future.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 14-Penalty for collecting excess sums.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is new, also. In a word, the provision contained in the section is that if any person collects a sum larger than that which he remits to the crown, the additional portion collected must go to the crown.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15-Time limited for prosecutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a new section. It is designed to permit the department to take action against defaulters or those who have falsified records in connection with taxes, under this act, within three years after the offence was committed. Without some similar proviso section 1142 of the criminal code precludes action in a case where the last falsification or fraudulent entry was made more than six months before it was discovered. As the departmental auditors do not audit the records of taxpayers as frequently as that nor is it possible for them to do so, the department is debarred from taking criminal action against defaulters, owing to the section of the criminal code referred to, a section which definitely limits such action to within six months from the time that the matter about which complaint has been made arose.
I think three years is too long. Why not make it two?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would take no exception to limiting the period to two years, except that I may point out that there is a similar provision in the Customs Act which names a period of three years, and there is always the overriding consideration that there can be no injustice done to the honest person.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-Definitions.

I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to section 122, coming under part XV. I received a wire this morning stating that there had been certain increases in the mint charges in regard to placer gold. Could the minister tell me what those charges are, or how they have been increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been a service charge imposed, applicable only to gold other than that with respect to which the premium tax of 25 per cent obtains. The cost of handling of small parcels of gold is much greater per ounce than the cost of handling gold in
Customs Tariff

large quantities at the mint. It is therefore provided that a service charge of one dollar per ounce shall obtain in the shipments of gold of fifteen ounces or less, but where the shipments are fifty ounces or more the service charge is 25 cents.
Might I ask further if the change in the imposition of this charge is as a result of the tax that was levied on gold, or was it imposed before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. There has been a service charge since March 19. It does not arise of necessity out of or have any relation to the tax on gold as introduced in the budget, but it is felt to be a fair service charge having regard to the disproportion as between the revenue derived from the shipments of gold which are not subject to the gold tax so called.

I know I am not exactly in order, Mr. Chairman, but there is one other question I wanted cleared up. Last year we had a good deal of congestion and delay in getting returns for our gold when it was shipped to the assay office at Vancouver. It has been alleged that there were certain reductions made in the staff of that office about the time of the peak of the production, and I should like to know from the minister if there is anything in that charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The difficulty does not arise, nor has it arisen, because of any action or lack of action on the part of the department in Canada, but delay very frequently arises through our having to await the assay returns when the gold is sold in the United States. In this connection may I also point out that the service charge of which I spoke a moment ago covers not only the cost of handling so far as the royal mint in Ottawa is concerned but the costs to which we are put on account of shipment charges, insurance, and an assay charge in the United States where the gold must again be assayed before payment is finally made.

speechtext:
Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 99, to amend the Income War Tax Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 1-Income.

Some time ago a statement was made before the committee that a certain gentleman was receiving $5,000 per week upon which he was not paying any income tax. I would be glad1 if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) could give us an explanation as to how he evaded the tax and if any amendments are being made to the act to deal with that situation.
Hon. E. N. RHODES Minister of Finance): The hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) will appreciate the delicacy of the question he submits in so far as it pertains to an individual. I may say to him that assuming there were sums received by an individual by way of instalments on a surplus in a company and which were really in effect an income, I believe the amendments which we have in the present bill will be ample to safeguard the treasury and give assurance that there will be no possibility of evading the proper payment of income tax by calling the payments something other than income.
I will indicate that section when we come to it.
I thank the hon. minister for his statement because I think this instance has created a great deal of ill feeling throughout the country.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 9 inclusive agreed to.
On section 10-Surplus distribution taxable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I ask the hon. member
for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) to look at this section. I may say to the committee that this

Income War Tax Act
section has been devised with very great care and in the light of the experience of years in the department. I have the hope, based upon the assurance which they have given me and the interpretation which has been placed upon this section by the Department of Justice, that its provisions will be ample to cover the case he indicated.
Will the provisions be retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, they will not be
retroactive. My hon. friend and the committee will recall full wejl some of the observations which have been made with respect to the retroactive features not only of this act but other taxing legislation. Apart from the injustice per se of retroactive legislation of this character, it involves the opening up of transactions which have been closed and concluded by the department and it creates difficulties of an administrative character which are almost insuperable. Eor these reasons it was thought that it would not be wise to ask for a retroactive feature in this section.

I understand that all
legislation in connection with income tax is retroactive to a certain extent. Legislation passed in one year is effective on the previous year's business or income and I assume that this section will be retroactive to that extent and apply to the income either for 1933 or for the expired portions of 1934.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The retroactive feature of which my hon. friend speaks has always been inherent to our income tax legislation since the date of its inception in 1917, and it would be a matter of great difficulty to avoid that feature. That phase of retroactiveness is not disturbed, altered or interfered with in any way by the amendment in question. When I spoke of it not being retroactive, I spoke in the sense that a transaction once having been closed and the tax paid we could not go back and bring it up again. That is an entirely different matter.

The minister has assured
us that this section 10 which we now have under review has been drafted with a great deal of care. Are we to assume that the other sections have not received the same grave attention from the draughtsmen?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not want that
interpretation to be taken from my having laid emphasis upon the fact that this section had been drafted with great care. I made that statement in connection with the remarks of the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) who made a particular point and perhaps I laid emphasis upon it by reason of the fact that this is a rather novel phase of income tax legislation. So far as I am aware, all the sections of this bill have been drafted with equal care but at the moment I happened to be dealing with this one particular section.

I should like to have
one point perfectly clear in my mind in connection with the time to which this particular section will apply. I am assuming that it will apply to the period of taxation since the filing of the last return by the person who might be involved in this particular transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My statement to the committee a short time ago was made after conference with the commissioner of income tax and I believe it is technically correct as it stands. But I did not refer to the variation in the degree of truth as exemplified by David Harum who said there were two kinds of truth, jury truth and gospel truth.
Which type is the minister's?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am advised that this,
not having hitherto been regarded as income under the terms of the act, will not be treated as income for the last year upon which income tax will be levied this year. In that sense it does not have a retroactive feature, it will only become operative from the time of its enactment. I hope I have made myself clear.
My particular point is this. This legislation is effective now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Assuming that the parties responsible under this particular section file their income tax returns as from the first of January, 1934, will it affect the particular income covered by this clause, from the first of January, 1934, until this date?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, for the reason that this was not income. It has only been made income in virtue of section 10 which we are now passing.
That was the point that appealed to me, and that is why I wanted to have it cleared up, because the minister did say that it would be retroactive to some extent and I did not think it would be.

I was interested to hear the minister say that this section would cover such instances as were outlined by the hon. member for Camrose. I would endorse
Income War Tax Act

the thought too that this should be made retroactive further back than the first of January. I remember that what I believe was called the business profits war tax act was passed a year or possibly two years after it was made operative. I recall that the business men in my own town had considerable difficulty making up the tax levied on them as I say, I am not sure whether it was one or two years after the money had been earned and spent. However, they were required by federal legislation to make up the tax to the federal treasury. It seems to me that if the act could be made retroactive in that case, to collect taxes from honest business men, it is only fair that the minister should devise ways and means of collecting the tax from such individuals as have evaded it. The instance has been cited of a person collecting more in one week, and paying nothing to the federal treasury, than many people collect in the entire year, and yet they have to pay income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take no exception to the desires expressed by my hon. friend from Kindersley but I must point out to him that in the year 1930 this house passed an amendment to the Income Tax Act which not only made it possible but actually extended an invitation to people to evade the income tax, which they did to the extent of hundreds of thousands of dollars. We are now taking a further step towards trying to repair the damage done at that time. If it were possible to pass an act which would meet an individual case such as my hon. friend no doubt has in mind, well and good; in that event we should be absolutely justified in applying the retroactive feature, in equity although not in strict legal right. Unfortunately however you have to devise a law of general application; it cannot be restricted to individuals; and when you devise a law of general application you run into numerous cases where moneys have been disbursed in conformity with the law and the tax paid to the extent the law called for. These transactions have been closed, the estates wound up, people are dead or have moved away and property is dispersed; so that it would be a physical impossibility to apply a law of that character; otherwise I would endeavour if it were at all possible t,o do so to devise an amendment which would meet the case my hon. friend has in mind.

May I remind the minister of the matter I raised a few weeks ago regarding the exemption of those who contribute towards unemployment relief funds. I suggested that amounts so contributed should be exempted from the income tax, the same as

contributions for charitable purposes. The minister said he would consider the suggestion sympathetically and look into the matter to see whether such exemptions could be made under the present regulations. May I ask him what steps he has taken in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a result of the representations made by my hon. friend I went into the matter with care with the commissioner of income tax. I looked over the regulations and found that, although my sympathy went out to him, in view of the object he had in mind, the fact was that if we attempted to devise regulations which would permit the avoidance of taxation to meet the case in point, assuming for the sake of discussion that it was an eminently worthy one, we should open the door to numerous cases of violation which might come technically within ,the wording that we might provide but which would be in effect an invitation to an evasion of the tax. Much therefore as I regret having to do so, I must inform my hon. friend that it is not possible by way of regulation to meet that specific case.

We are assuming now that too many people are dishonest in making out their income tax statements. But there is another point that suggests itself here. These very people to whom I have been referring give a fairly large proportion of their wages to help their fellow members when unemployed, so as to keep them off public relief. This is a voluntary obligation they undertake, and the chances are that another year they will refuse to assume this obligation to maintain members of organizations on relief, with the result that such persons as are helped by these voluntary contributions will hereafter become recipients of public relief. That is another way of looking at the matter. The government has been saving a fairly large sum of money through the amounts contributed voluntarily in this way, and the answer which the minister gives is rather disappointing, because I am afraid it may have the effect I suggest. I believe that had the minister given to this suggestion the same careful consideration that he gave to other classes, he could have found ways and means of exempting these people from taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that I gave just as much consideration, if not more, to the case he has submitted, for the reason that it is one that naturally arouses one's sympathy, which is not so as regards the incident mentioned by my hon. friends from Camrose and Kindersley. I venture to

Tricorne War Tax Act
say however that if the hon. gentleman were in my place, charged with the responsibility that attaches to a ministerial office, he would have come to precisely the same decision as I was compelled to come to for the reasons I have indicated. The statement I originally made holds with respect to this case, but I may point out to my hon. friend that he weakened rather than strengthened his case when in his second remarks he referred to the fact that this was a passing phase that would obtain only for a year or two. It would be very bad legislation to attempt to put something permanent into the form of a statute which was admittedly designed to cover an ephemeral case.

I have a question to ask
the minister, and while it may not be under this section it has reference to taxation. A year ago an amendment was passed for the purpose of collecting a tax on bearer bonds. There was a regulation to identify the bond, but I have reason to believe that some of these bonds were handed in by different people. For instance, John Brown -I am not referring to our hon. friend here- might take in bonds that belong to some other person. I am told that has been done. I would suggest that while this bill is being dealt with perhaps that point could be covered, have it arranged that not only the bearer of the bond be identified but the absolute owner be identified at the bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The case indicated by my hon. friend is clearly one of fraud. The statute must of necessity assume that the law will be properly observed. The case he mentions is one for the criminal court. May I point out that until the department becomes thoroughly experienced in dealing with these certificates some little delay is bound to occur, and possibly a slip here and there. When I say that at the moment there are in the department over two million of these certificates, it will be apparent that the mere physical act of sorting and allocating and computing them involves a tremendous amount of clerical work. I have no doubt there will be instances of the law being evaded, yet slowly but surely the strings will tighten, and the individual who thinks to-day that he escapes will find out one or two or perhaps three years hence that his escape was imaginary and not real; ultimately he will be called upon to pay the full amount of the tax that the law calls for.

I have been told by tax
auditors that they knew of cases of evasion. It seems to me there might be some tightening up by the Finance department. While I am on my feet I would ask if the minister can give the committee figures or an estimate of what amount of money that little amendment meant to the exchequer of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The five per cent tax as
a whole brought in somewhere in the neighbourhood of $4,800,000 last year. I have no doubt that that sum will be increased proportionately as the years go by, because there are always difficulties in administering a new act which covers so much ground and involves so much accounting and has so many ramifications. But even that sum is an indication of the merits of the proposals put through a year ago. I may point out that you cannot make a perfect act, you will always find men who are criminally inclined and who can evade almost any law in part. I think for instance of the tax on cheques. At one time cheques below $5 were exempt. One individual of some substance, and who is regarded as a good citizen, when he had a $15 account to pay was at pains to issue three $5 cheques. You will have those cases and it is difficult to legislate so as to avoid them. They do not indicate a weakness in the law, I would rather incline to the view that they indicate a weakness in human nature which we must always take into account.
One more word. The minister mentioned that it involves a large amount of extra work but he will agree that it gives employment, and the government has been very well paid for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.

Would it not save a lot of
that trouble if in future no bearer bonds were issued? Is there any particular reason why there should be bearer bonds? If there were not it would save an infinity of trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That suggestion is worthy
of consideration, but it would tend to a frozen situation with respect to bonds which would make financial transactions very difficult, not being negotiable. I am afraid it would be almost impossible to comprehend a situation of that character.
Registered bonds are negotiable now, you have only to sign a transfer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are not negotiable in the sense of passing from hand to hand. They require the same formality as any other transaction, an entry both ways. I shall be glad to give consideration to the suggestion but I doubt very much if it would be feasible.
Income War Tax Act

A man does not pay his debts with a hundred dollar bond. Bonds are only sold through a bank. There would not be as much trouble in transferring them as there is in making out the certificate every time you get a coupon cashed and it would do away with all the chances of evasion.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 11 agreed to.
On section 12-Advances to nonresident corporation without compensation.

I notice that this and many of the succeeding sections refer to people and companies outside of Canada. I was wondering if the minister could make a general statement covering the situation and also advising whether the legislation is reciprocal with other countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is rather difficult to make a general statement. While these sections are general in effect, I may say that they have arisen because of some cases met with in actual experience, where attempts have been made to evade the law by a subsidiary company lending its money to the parent company without interest; also in connection with the five per cent tax, which was only applicable in cases where the payment was in Canadian funds. We soon found that in certain instances, in order to avoid paying that tax, companies made provision for their payments to be made in foreign funds. We are amending the act to meet that case as well.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 13 agreed to.
On section 14-Nonresidents deemed to be carrying on business.

I notice we are going to tax nonresident companies doing business in Canada. The question arises in my mind as to what method we are going to adopt to collect the tax. Assuming that the salesman for a United States company comes into Canada and does business, we now propose to charge them income tax. How we are to collect the tax is what concerns me at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In practically every instance these companies have assets in Canada or have receivables in Canada or they wish to continue in business in Canada. So that in any one of the three cases, or a combination of them, there is a situation which enables the department to ensure that it will receive the tax in precisely the same way as it would in the case of a Canadian company.

Does the government
possess any particular information as to what companies are doing business in Canada? Would they get that through the present income tax offices, or would they have access say to the customs department for that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The department has a very comprehensive tax roll which pretty well covers the ground. I have no doubt that from time to time an individual or perhaps a company may be found that is not on the list, but sooner or later they arrive there.

For example, assume that some companies in the United States are selling lumber in Canada, they may sell a greater or less quantity. Is it the intention of the government to watch the sales of such products coming into Canada and collect income tax on that basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they have agents or an agency or employees in Canada, then the department would apply the tax. I might point out to my hon. friend, who has had experience in these matters, that any business worthy of the name is bound to make its presence apparent, either through office telephones, the receipt of telegrams or in other ways. All these sources of information are available to the department and are combed and watched very carefully.

I wonder whether it is
the purpose of the government, where a foreign company has agents in Canada, regardless of the volume of business that may be done by those agents, to have a return filed with the department as to the amount of business done by each agent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, in practice what
happens is this : The department gets in touch with the company and has the company, through one agent or through its own officers at the head office, file the necessary income tax form.
I am just a little cloudy as to this feature. Would that result in every foreign company doing business in Canada having to file a return with the income tax department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if they have an agency or place of business in Canada.

I would point out to
the minister that practically every company doing business in Canada has an agency in some form. It may be a commission or a salaried agency, but they have agencies of some kind; otherwise it would be very un-

Income War Tax Act
likely that any business would result. Just for a moment I am going to ask the minister to visualize every company shipping goods to Canada filing a return with the Canadian government, and the effect that will have on the interchange of business between Canada and other countries. I assume that if this legislation is not reciprocal at the present time it will be only a very short time until that situation results. I feel that it will be only a very short time until all producers in Canada will be filing returns with the various governments all over the world with which they have to do business. To me that is an impossible situation. I believe my opinion of this particular section would be that the cost of procuring the information and of administering the act would be much greater than the income that would be received, but even if that were not the fact I think the interference with international business that this will bring about will create an impression that we in Canada cannot afford to create at the present time.
I do not like to refer to the policies of the government; I realize that they have difficulty in procuring funds, but I do believe the government should very seriously consider or reconsider any suggestion that is going to interfere in any way with the exchange of our goods with the other nations of the world. We have enough difficulties to-day. I am not anxious to see goods kept out of Canada; 1 am much more anxious to see goods go from Canada. I look for reciprocal regulations on the part of other nations when we expect their nationals to file returns with the Canadian government and to pay taxes in Canada as well as in their own country. I believe the minister would do very well to reconsider this legislation before he puts it on our statute books.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is practically a truism that any form of taxation interferes with business; we can start from that promise. It seems to me the only consideration, apart from the necessity of revenue and of fair application of the tax, is to be found in the answer to the query as to whether a tax in itself is fair.
I do not agree with my hon. friend that this form of taxation will interfere with business any more than any other form of taxation. May I point out in the first place that the general principle of this taxation is found in practically every country. Furthermore the occasion which led us, in the first instance, to apply the five per cent tax was that we found foreign countries benefiting through their treasury receiving a portion of the 74726-254
revenue which properly should come to this country. It does not cost the individual company or taxpayer any more to pay five per cent in Canada than it would to pay that amount in some other country. As a result of our taxation of last year we have diverted to the Canadian treasury sums of money which hitherto have gone by way of taxation into the treasuries of foreign countries.
So far as interfering with foreign business is concerned, may I point out to my hon. friend that subsection (3) of section 14 provides :
The governor in council shall have power to exempt from the operation of this section the income in whole or in part of residents of any country which enters into reciprocal agreement with Canada to exempt the income of residents of Canada earned in such country.
The very wording of that subsection will indicate to my hon. friend and the committee that we had in mind the desire not only not to interfere with but to make it convenient to expedite business transactions as between people in this country and people in foreign countries.
This is a revenue tax?

I had particularly noted the reciprocal provision in subsection (3) just mentioned by the Minister of Finance. The only interpretation I can place upon this clause is that it is a further attempt on the part of this government to deepen the channel by which they are going to direct business to certain countries and away from other countries. There can be no other interpretation placed upon it. We will enter into reciprocal agreements with those countries with which we wish to do business, but those countries with which we do not wish to do business we will make subject to this income tax. Evidently no consideration whatever has been given to the fact that foreign companies doing business in Canada and selling their products to consumers in Canada, if they are to pay a tax to the Canadian government, must and will add that tax to what the Canadian consumer must pay. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance also if he can tell this house of any precedent for this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the fears of my hon. friend are entirely unfounded. He will be surprised to know that this proposal did not emanate from the government at all; it emanated from the commissioner of income tax. Because of his experience, and because of his advice, which was accepted, the government, of course, is only too happy to sponsor this proposal. -It has no reference

Income War Tax Act

to trade at all; it is purely a question of taxation, and it recognizes a principle which we have recognized hitherto in our own statutes. With all due deference to my hon. friend I must say that I do not understand his apprehension either with respect to the question of trade or that of policy. Certainly when I first discussed this matter with the officials of the department that view was not present in my mind, but the action was taken solely with a view to making our taxation proposals uniform and fair and to bring into the treasury every dollar which could properly be brought in. It was done for those reasons, and those reasons alone.
I directed a question to the Minister of Finance which I believe he has answered in the negative. I asked him as to whether or not there was in any other country any precedent for this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The commissioner of income tax informs me that this principle is found in the taxation of practically every country, and so far as it obtains with respect to the principle of double taxation it has been recognized through the fiscal committee of the League of Nations, and has been the *ubject of action by them.

I am glad to have the assurance from the Minister of Finance that the commissioner of income tax is the culprit in this particular case because I consider that this is culpable legislation. Under the circumstances I should be pleased if the minister would allow the section to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no objection to allowing it to stand, but I may say that the government will insist upon its passage. When I mentioned the commissioner of income tax I did not refer to him with the intention of evading any responsibility but merely for the purpose of disillusioning my hon. friend from the hallucination under which he seemed to be labouring, namely, that there was some dire purpose in this legislation. Otherwise I should not have mentioned the name of the commissioner of income tax. I assume full responsibility- and so does the government-and unless my hon. friend has some special purpose in asking that the section stand I would ask him not to insist. Of course, if he has reasons I will accede to his request without any hesitancy.

As I have not been disillusioned I should prefer to have the section stand.	,
Section stands.
Section 15 agreed to.

On section 16-Transfers to minors.

May I ask the minister if the same principle he laid down with regard to the section dealing with what I may call disguised revenue will apply? In other words, shall this be made retroactive in the sense that the revenues derived heretofore on values transferred in the past will fall under this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course my hon. friend is aware of the purpose of the section.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is to prevent evasion, but it will not be retroactive. It will apply only to those instances which happen after the passage of this legislation, in precisely the same manner as was the case in connection with section 10.
That is, to transfers made after this is passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Acting Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose on February 23, we were discussing the question as to whether or not power should be given to constables or fishery inspectors or customs officers not only to seize wrongly or incorrectly labelled canned fish, but also to confiscate them with a right of appeal to the minister in favour of the party aggrieved. Strong objections w'ere made against the provision giving a power of confiscation to the officers and in the light of the discussion a new clause has been drafted to cover the points at issue. I believe the amendment is satisfactory to those hon. members who objected. I shall ask one of my colleagues to move it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Move it yourself.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The section as
amended would read as follows:
27. Any cqn of fish or shell fish that bears any false or misleading mark or that is

Meat and Canned Foods Act
incorrectly labelled or marked and not labelled or marked in accordance with this act, or with the regulations made thereunder, may be seized by an inspector or by any customs, excise or police officer, or by any constable, and shall be confiscated to His Majesty by any two justices of the peace, or by any magistrate having the power of two justices of the peace, if it is found that the label or marking is intended or calculated to deceive.
In other words, we are taking away from the officers the right or power to confiscate, and giving it to two justices of the peace or a magistrate having the powers of two justices of the peace. I move that section 1 in the bill be amended by deleting section 27 appearing therein, and substituting therefor the words I have indicated.

I think the purpose of the
amendment is quite right but I would point out that the minister has left out the first three lines of the section. If you are going to delete the whole section, and not merely amend it, you will have to put in the first three lines beginning with "Section twenty-seven," or if you are just going to amend it, the amendment will begin with "27."

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, starting from the number "27."

Would the minister
inform the committee how many prosecutions have been taken in the past under this law. Were there many causes of complaint?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I think there were
some prosecutions, but the law as it now exists is not stringent enough. As my hon. friend knows, there are many kinds of salmon fish. There are, for instance, six species of salmon: sockeyes, red, pink and white springs; cohoes; steelhead; pink, and chum, and some of these species are worth two or three times as much as others, as my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi is well aware. Hence the temptation to label inferior quality goods wrongly. We think that this legislation is absolutely necessary'. Up to date we have been able to control canned fish retailed on the market in Canada, but we could not do anything with regard to exported goods, and by' this legislation we are seeking to prevent the export of falsely labelled canned fish. I think that is in the best interests of our market abroad.

Are there any special
police officers to enforce this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
No, our fishery
officers.

How are you going to prove the intention? I have no objection to the words "calculated to deceive."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That expression occurs
in many sections of our criminal code. The justices will have to be convinced there is the intent and that the label is capable of deception.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

And the intent is
derived from the facts, and it is for the justices to decide.

It will prevent both?

Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 95, to amend the Roy'al Canadian Mounted Police Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Stirling in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I might offer a word in explanation of this bill, Mr. Chairman. To sum it up, it is to permit constables of the Roy'al Canadian Mounted Police to make

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
provision for their widows and children solely out of contributions made by them. This will be part 4 of the Mounted Police Act. Part 3 provides that a constable after a certain service shall receive a pension for himself. Part 2 provides that officers shall receive pensions and that on their death their widows and children shall receive one-half the amount that the officers would have been entitled to. But we have no provision whatever in our law with respect to the widows and children of constables, and the proposal is that constables be permitted to create a fund under the control of the government, and that out of that fund pensions be paid to the widows and children in accordance with the table set out in this bill.
The whole amount is contributed by the men themselves. These tables have been prepared by actuaries in the Department of Insurance, and by the officials of the treasury, and the proposal has been reported as actuarially sound and as being able to carry itself. But there is an express provision in the bill that, no moneys shall be paid out of the public funds of Canada in respect of this measure. The fund must carry itself.

While my question does not come under this bill probably, it comes under the minister's department. I would ask if it is the policy of the department to pay special officers as well as to allow them to receive moieties of fines? Where an officer is told by his commanding officer to look after the Excise Act, does he receive pay as well as part of the moities?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The officers do not receive the moieties, they go into a trust fund.

I should like to draw the
attention of the minister to a practice which has occurred, I understand more than once in British Columbia. This particular case happened in May. Two officers of the force first sold a man some liquor and then laid an information against him. They were severely reprimanded by the magistrate who called it conspiracy of a most diabolical nature. That may be rather strong language but I think such a practice should be discontinued. We have cases where under cover men are sent out to endeavour to purchase drinks but in this case the officers deliberately tried to sell liquor to a man and laid an information. This incident occurred at Richmond in May of this year, and I think such practices should be stopped.
TMr. Guthrie.]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The members of the police would receive no part of that fine if an award was made, that would go into the trust fund. I will report the remarks of my hon. friend to the commissioner for his consideration.

Section 77 agreed to.

Do the patrol boats come
under the Department of Justice or the Department of National Revenue?

speechtext:
The patrol boats in the
preventive service come under the mounted police.

This may be a little out of order but I ask the committee to excuse me while I draw the attention of the minister to something which I think should be remedied immediately. On the eleventh of this month a foreign vessel came into the harbour of Shippigan and called for a pilot. There are two licensed pilots at that port, one of which has a boat and the other has not. I shall have an inquiry
made into the incident and when I receive a report I will submit it to my hon. friend.

Is the time served with the provincial government counted towards the pension of a man absorbed into the new forces?

The house resumed from Tuesday, May 3, consideration in committee of Bill No. 70, to amend the Food and Drugs Act.
On section 1-Regulations by governor in council.

speakeroldname: Hon. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while there has been considerable discussion on this bill and especially in connection with the second amendment, the first
amendment has not yet been considered. It is for the committee to decide whether we shall continue with the second amendment first or take them in order.
Probably it is well to begin with section 1 in the regular order. This amendment makes provision for regulation by order in council to add to or take from those names that appear in schedule A, the number of diseases or symptoms of diseases, and to add to or take from the list of remedies-material it is called there-of various kinds found in the act, such as sera, remedies of a poisonous nature, and so forth. The object of the amendment is to give flexibility to the administration of the act. No doubt from time to time increase in scientific knowledge renders changes desirable, and this amendment empowers the minister to recommend changes in consequence of such developing knowledge.

When this bill was
introduced the minister explained that the object was to bring the Food and Drugs Act into conformity with what is usually called the P.P.M. Act, that is to say, the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act. I have no quarrel with that purpose; indeed, the last time the committee sat I intimated that I agreed with that principle. But I made certain observations that I am now going to repeat, with all deference to the minister, for whom I have the kindliest feeling, and whom I must thank for the courtesy he has shown me in allowing me to discuss the matter with his very efficient officials. To my mind this is not the proper way to proceed at all. The Food and Drugs Act is a very important piece of legislation, and so is the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act. We have passed may important measures this session, but this act relates to national health, and I submit that we ought to give this whole matter all the consideration to which it is entitled; not- that I wish to imply that the minister and his officials have not given it proper consideration, but in this committee it should receive greater attention than the procedure which we are about to adopt contemplates.
In order to bring this act into conformity with the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act, I suggest that the latter act in its entirety should be revamped. It has not been touched for many years, and the procedure now proposed will not bring the Food and Drugs Act into conformity with the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act, because in that act there do not appear any dispositions similar
to 18

to those which it is sought in this amendment to introduce into the Food and Drugs Act.
National health is of course of very great importance, and I wish to discuss certain phases of this bill. In the first place, section 1 provides that subsection 1 of section 3 of the Food and Drugs Act shall be amended by:
adding to or removing from the list contained in schedule A hereto such abnormal physical states....
First of all, I would point out that there is no place where I or anyone else can go to determine what an abnormal physical state is; that is something that is purely in the estimation either of the minister or of his officials. There is no definition either in the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act or in the Food and Drugs Act of what constitutes an abnormal physical state. And further by:
-adding to or removing from schedule B hereto such material-
Now, "schedule B hereto" contains no "material;" it is only the nomenclature or description of the abnormal physical states. The hon. member for St. Boniface hands me a schedule from the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act, and in that act there is no schedule B. The section reads:
Subsection 1 of section 3 of the Food and Drugs Act, chapter 76 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, is amended by adding thereto the following paragraph immediately after paragraph (h) thereof.
The Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act is not chapter 76 of the revised statutes, and in the Food and Drugs Act there is no schedule wherein "material" is defined. In that respect therefore the section is badly drawn. In the second place, there is nothing that defines material. "Such material;" what material? What is material? That ought to be defined somewhere. It is "such material, as may be deemed by the minister to be necessary in the public interest."
I submit with all deference and kindliness that this is going much too far. It is indeed going much too far. I understand it is a matter of national health, and with the general principle of the bill I have no quarrel, but I think we are going much too far afield by giving power to the minister whereby at any time he may remove from or add to or otherwise deal with the schedule listing these abnormal physical states. Surely if an abnormal physical state develops in a certain locality it does not demand immediate medical intervention, it is not a state of war, it does not necessitate that the cabinet sit at once and deal with it, it does not require

that the minister should at once add to or subtract from the list. This proposal means disruption of the whole pharmaceutical trade. People have been in the habit of dealing with certain medical products, and all at once that is to be stopped, with no provision here, although there may be something in a comer of the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act to say upon what terms it may be done and what kind of notice will be given or to what interests and what rights will be safeguarded. Suppose the minister finds another abnormal physical state and lists it in this schedule and then prohibits the sale of certain medicines which may be sold to-day for all abnormal physical states not mentioned in the schedule. Then the whole thing is topsy-turvy. So I submit that so far as that is concerned the amendment goes much too far and that that section should not be concurred in.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: To which one does the hon. member refer?

I refer to section 1 of the amendment. If the minister wants to insist upon certain things to make this act conform with the other, surely he is going much too far in asking for that power. Not that I fear that he will not administer it in the public interest, but that it will be creating untold hardship for those who deal in these products. To put it clearly, if the schedule goes through as it is-and I hope it will not, because I shall submit certain amendments, and the minister should decide that cancer- to take an extreme case-should come out of the schedule, immediately that would disturb the trade. Suppose the minister should say that grippe should be included in that schedule, there is no notice given to anybody, then all those who have prepared specifics for that ailment immediately fall under the law. The minister, I think quite properly, has given notice that this bill shall not come into force until January 1 of next year. In all kindliness let me say that there is no great rush to put this measure through; why not let it stand until the next session of parliament, and in the meantime notify those interests which may be affected to make representations if they desire? If the minister does that I believe he will get much better legislation than if he tries to put this bill through now, because as I see it there is not one particle of all this that will bring this Food and Drugs Act into conformity with the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act. Even if it did I submit it is wrong in practice because the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act should be revamped from top to bottom.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes, but very soon after. It is not proper to describe this as a hole in the corner business at all. If there is one thing necessary with regard to public health it is publicity. We are trying to do something in the proper way; our object is to inform the people, and there is no hole in the corner business about it at all. Now, coming back to this point, I say there is a considerable degree of conformity brought about by this amendment, by adopting the same list of diseases and conditions that now exists under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act. That is a material gain. What is the reason for all this? It has been found that in some cases when the manufacturer or seller of a patent medicine has been stopped from selling it under the one act he has proceeded to sell it under the other, and we wish to have the same list apply to both acts so that we may have uniform administration. Especially I wish to direct attention to the fact that the amendment explains this situation. When my hon. friend refers to material it does not refer to diseases but to actual remedies which are enumerated there.

I do not see any great cause for confusion in this legislation. The minister has told us that the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act forbids the sale of drugs or remedies having to do with certain diseases, and that certain individuals have been avoiding that law by purchasing or selling these articles under the Food and Drugs Act. I think the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act is absolutely correct in forbidding the sale of stated remedies under label for the alleviation and cure of a great many, in fact most, of the diseased conditions that we find in schedule A, which is a new schedule being inserted into the Food and Drugs Act. On the other hand I do feel that to forbid individuals to purchase certain remedies for more or less trivial conditions is rather an arbitrary stand to take.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: What are the trivial conditions? fMr. Chevrier.]

If the minister will just give me a moment I will run over the list. On the other hand, after looking over this list I find that there is no danger in the world of people seeking to buy remedies, or of others attempting to sell them, for a great many of the conditions set out in this list. There are one or two conditions with which I must confess, though with some hesitation, the regular practice of medicine has had seemingly but slight success, and for which various patent remedies-call them quacks if you like-seem to have been able to afford the relief we have not been able to bring about. I would mention first epilepsy, to which I propose to refer at a little greater length in a moment.
Now let us look over this list of diseases for which no one is permitted to import, manufacture, offer for sale, advertise by any means whatever or sell any remedy which is supposed to relieve or cure the conditions enumerated; let us consider the conditions one by one, starting with alcoholism. The only danger to an individual seeking relief from alcoholism by remedies that might be prescribed by a druggist, who is the only individual who would prescribe remedies, is that he might get rather too heavy a dose of one of the hypnotics. There is an extremely remote danger that he might get a sufficiently heavy dose to put him out, but the danger is very slight. Ordinarily speaking, the remedies the druggist would sell for the relief of alcoholism would cause no great danger. They would not do very much good, nor would they do much harm, so that the person buying the remedy would be no farther ahead and he would be out only the price of the remedy.
We now come to appendicitis. When a person has an honest to goodness attack of appendicitis he does not monkey with it. He is genuinely sick, and of that fact there can be no doubt in the world. He is not going to run to a drug store when the pain in his side is causing him such agony that he can scarcely bear it, and under those circumstances he will not be asking for a cure from a druggist. If the person affected knows he has appendicitis he is certainly not going to bother with a drug store and, believe me, if the druggist knows it is appendicitis he will not offer any relief. He will chase that person to the best doctor to be found, and will have him go as fast as possible. So, as far as appendicitis is concerned this measure is ineffective, and it is all bunkum to assume that anybody suffering from appendicitis will take a chance with patent remedies or common salts.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
Then, we come to arteriosclerosis. Well, just how a druggist or a layman is going to know when a person is suffering from arteriosclerosis I cannot guess. It takes a pretty fair doctor to diagnose this disease, which is commonly known as hardening of the arteries. I should not think there would be a great deal of danger of anybody running to a drug store or to anybody else and saying, "here, sell me something to cure my arteriosclerosis." In that respect the legislation is a joke.
Now we come to blood poisoning. Well,
I grant you that the laity, the people generally, have the idea that every little infected wound they may have on their hands or their toes, together with a few streaks running up their arms or legs, constitute blood poisoning. But that is not so. Those conditions are called lymphangitis, or inflammation of the lymph channels, and if very much aggravated or neglected that condition might possibly lead to blood poisoning. But blood poisoning is a condition in which there are live, active, microbe organisms in the blood. For that reason it is a severe and serious disease, and when a person is suffering from it he shakes and shivers in his bed sufficiently to rattle the windows in the bedroom. A person suffering in that way is not going to go to a druggist and ask for relief. That also is a joke; there is no question about it. If a person is suffering from blood poisoning he will employ all the doctors he can afford in order to see what chance he has to live.
The next disease mentioned is Bright's disease. About two-thirds of us have Bright's disease after we reach the age of forty or fifty years. Of course, we may have it in lesser degrees, but if it appears in severe or aggravated form the less medicine that is taken the better, and when a person has a serious attack he does not bother with a druggist. He is panting for life and for breath, and he will call a doctor. The only remedy I can imagine a druggist would dare sell a person suffering from Bright's disease would be Epsom salts, or something like that, and if they did not do him any good they would do no harm. For those reasons I cannot see that this bill can have much effect so far as Bright's disease is concerned.
Then we come to cancer, and at this point we must pause to consider. A person may have a little sore on the corner of his mouth which has been neglected and which may develop into a cancer. The sore may appear at the corner of his eye or he may have had a sudden difficulty with his digestion. All these conditions might come out of a perfectly clear sky. Then, a woman may develop a sore on a nipple, a breast or other places. There is no danger of her going to a druggist. She may go to a quack doctor and have an arsenic plaster put on, or something of that kind. But there would be no danger of her going to a druggist and asking for relief for cancer. It is my implicit belief that if a person knows he has cancer he will not go to a druggist and ask for a remedy but will consult the best doctor he can find or can afford to employ and receive the best advice he can pay for. I believe a druggist would not have the nerve to sell a remedy for cancer. He could not possibly do so.
Now we come to diabetes. It is not difficult to tell when one is suffering from diabetes. We are not giving a medical clinic and we shall not discuss this disease at length, but I cannot imagine anyone with honest-to-good-ness diabetes tampering with his welfare to the extent of going to a drug store for relief. Then, in these days we have the Banting remedy of insulin, and for that reason diabetes is viewed from an entirely different standpoint. There was a time when this disease was considered beyond help, and in drug stores here and there and all over all sorts of patent remedies were sold to effect cures. But because of the scientific advances made in connection with this disease, and the discovery by Sir Frederick Banting, that condition has been stopped. For those reasons diabetes may be scratched off the list.
Now we come to diphtheria-and in this instance we have a case no one should monkey with. Here is a time when no one should monkey with a druggist. This is one disease which could be left on the list, and we could call it diphtheria, sore throat or whatever you like. Just as soon as a child has a real honest-to-goodness sore throat, get a doctor. Call a sore throat diphtheria, and get a doctor, and we would have less deaths. I would say we could include ordinary sore throats, and prevent druggists from selling remedies for infectious sore throats, whether they be diphtheria, tonsilitis, scarlet fever, Ludwig's angina, or anything of the kind.
Now we come to dropsy. Dropsy is a symptom, not a disease and occurs in connection with Bright's disease, heart disease, liver disease and all sorts of diseases in which the limbs, and preeminently the legs, swell up to a point where, by pressure from a finger, pits may be formed. Here, again, if a druggist had the hardiness to prescribe for dropsy, and decided to prescribe Epsom salts which he

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
likely would do, he would probably be suggesting about as good a remedy as he could in any case.
And now we come to the next important one, namely epilepsy. I said a little while ago that unfortunately the medical profession has had no success with epilepsy. We have prescribed all sorts of medicines. We have performed counter depressions on the brain and taken out a piece of the skull. We have done all sorts of things. Here and there we have effected a cure, and here and there our efforts have been fruitless. But there are individuals, quacks if you like-and I do not call them that disrespectfully, because I believe in rendering unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's-who have evidently found means to relieve epilepsy. As a medical man with thirty years' experience I believe in letting people get relief or cures where they can get them. If a doctor cannot give it to them, let them go where they can get it. That is my policy. It might be worth the while of this committee to listen to a letter or two that I have. I have half a dozen, but I shall not read them all. This one is an appeal to the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, and it says:
Dear Sir,-
It was brought to my notice that a new Canadian law has been proposed, which will make it impossible for a person to obtain treatment for epilepsy attacks except through a physician. I refer to the bill sponsored by the Hon. Dr. Murray MacLaren, Minister of Pensions and National Health. Now I myself have suffered from epilepsy since 1923. I tried the home doctor and others, spending hundreds of dollars in vain. Then I used the treatment from the Western Medical Corporation of Chicago-
I do not know anything about them personally:
Now I am feeling fine. If this new law comes into force I understand I cannot buy medicines from any concern either in the United States or in Canada. This rvould mean that I cannot get my medicine and would probably mean worse than death to me, as epilepsy works on the brain.
That is true, Epilepsy developing in early years usually leaves a fumbling, feeble brain after the child grows up, and the longer you have epilepsy the foolisher you get.

-if people are suffering from epilepsy and can get no relief except through taking medicine or going to quack doctors, let them get it that way. Now as to erysipelas. Erysipelas is something that should not be tampered or fooled with, but I think there is little. danger of one suffering from erysipelas losing much valuable time because it spreads so rapidly and the individual becomes so prostrated with illness in a short time that he will not temporize very long with tomfool measures; he will call in a physician on his own account.
