relief from this condition. I do not see the force of putting those diseases on the list because certainly a person with an attack of gall stone, colic or real colic is not going to temporize with drugs, He will be yelling his head off until the doctor comes along with a hypodermic syringe and gives him some relief.
As to gangrene, a part that becomes gangrenous is intensely painful. It becomes very red at first, then blue, then black. It is usually terrifying enough in its phenomena to drive any person to call in a doctor if there is a doctor to be had. If any person knows he has gangrene he will not seek patent remedies or any light measures to relieve him. There is no question in the world but
that he will by some means or other obtain the advice and assistance of a medical man.
As to gastric and duodenal ulcers, people who are suffering from these would often be safer to stay away from the doctor, because it is not- always certainly known when a person has a gastric or duodenal ulcer, and it is not always certain what is the best treatment. The only symptons would be a very aggravated form of dyspepsia. I suppose anybody with a very aggravated form of dyspepsia might go to a druggist, and if he asked for something for a gastric or duodenal ulcer the druggist might give him a little sodium and bismuth, which would certainly do no harm. But sooner or later he finds his way to a medical man. When he does so he may get a diagnosis or he may receive the relief which he desires. I cannot see any real reason why this should be allowed to remain on the list, except that if a person goes to a druggist or a chemist for a remedy for gastric or duodenal ulcers, the chemist should be forced to send him to a medical man. The same thing applies all down the list.
In the case of goitre, a druggist may take it upon himself to prescribe iodine of potash, or he might prescribe iodine in some form. He may suggest that the goitre be painted with iodine, but that would not do the patient very much good. Iodine of potash might relieve the patient but I cannot see much danger in allowing this disease to remain on the list. If the patient has an aggravated goitre which upsets his nervous system or if his breath is shut off he will soon call in a doctor. Until that time arrives there is no great danger.
Many people have heart disease without knowing it. When the time comes that they realize they have it, there is no question about the matter. They are not going to temporize with either a quack or a druggist, they are going to see a medical man in an effort to get the needed relief.
The next is high blood pressure. The point in connection with the entire list is:	How is
an individual to know he has got blood pressure without consulting a medical man? How is he to know that he has infantile paralysis without consulting a medical man? How is he to know he has lockjaw? By the time he has lockjaw he will surely know it, and a medical man will not be of much use to him. In the case of locomotor ataxia there is no danger, but there may be some in the case of obesity. An individual may temporize with a lot of drugs which would do him no good. The next are pleurisy, pneumonia, ruptures and scarlet fever. I do not see a great deal of danger in any of those but scarlet fever. The averag" individual

becomes so sick with scarlet fever that he seeks a medical man. There are a few cases which are so mild that they are not detected and there is great danger of the spreading of the infection. If such a case is not sufficiently severe to make itself known to the individual or to his family, it is not very likely that a druggist would notice his condition. In such a case an individual is not going to go to a druggist or a quack and ask for a remedy for scarlet fever. In the case of severe scarlet fever there will be no temporizing, the individual will call in a medical man.
There is no danger with spinal meningitis, but there is some in connection with trachoma. Trachoma is chronic granulated eyelids and there is danger not only to the individual's eyesight but through the spreading of the disease to anyone who might use the same towel or wash-cloth. Tuberculosis, tumors, typhoid fever-I do not see much danger in connection with any of those. In connection with venereal disease there is a great deal of danger. While it is not very often that an individual will apply to a druggist for the relief of this disease, this is one disease which should be left on the list. It should be underlined with a heavy line. Any druggist who takes it upon himself to prescribe for venereal trouble should be severely punished. Venereal disease is one of the conditions which is undermining the health of the nation and it should receive more attention than it is receiving from the Department of Pensions and National Health.
That is why they cut off the grant.

I suppose so. This legislation if adopted will create a definite and decided hardship to a class of invalids whom the doctors have been unable to assist, a class of invalids who have been able to get relief by other means, a class of invalids to whom this parliament or anybody else has not the right to deny relief so long as they can find it. For these reasons I appeal to the minister to have epilepsy taken off the list. The class of remedies sold to these people may do them no good, but they do them no harm. We medical men cannot do them any good and for this reason I think epilepsy Should be left off the list.
I have nothing but endorsation for the provision that the minister shall have the authority to add to or remove from schedule B such material as he may assume to be necessary in the public interests. The schedule reads:

Preparations of strophantlius, digitalis, ergot and any other vegetable preparations for which biological tests are deemed necessary.

Preparations of pituitrin, thyroid, adrenalin and any other animal tissue preparations.
There is not much danger that any individual is going to submit to a hypodermic injection of something about which he knows nothing. I do not intend to read the balance, but I see no reason why the minister should not have entire control. The absurd part of the bill is this long list of disease conditions in connection with which people are not to be allowed to apply to other than medical men for relief. I do not consider that there is any danger but that ninety-nine per cent of the people suffering from these diseases will appeal to medical men for relief.

of these drugs by drug stores?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I cannot reply comprehensively, yes or no. Drug stores can sell these remedies to physicians or physicians can prescribe them through a druggist.

Suppose I have been
treated in the past by a physician who has informed me that a particular medicine will do me good. I go and ask a druggist to sell me that medicine, without telling him precisely what I want it for. Is the druggist permitted to sell it? I am interested in this matter, personally interested, because I am interested in the drug business, and I want to know whether I am violating the law or not. The largest drug store in northern New Brunswick is under the jurisdiction of my son, who is a medical doctor, and of his brother, who is a pharmacist.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: You are a doctor yourself.

Not a medical doctor; I
cannot give a prescription. I want to know, in the interest of the business, whether we are violating the law or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Whether you are
violating the law if this bill is passed?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Under this proposed
amendment these remedies can either be manufactured in Canada or they can be imported from abroad.
By a druggist?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
By anyone. The point
in regard to labelling is an important one. One of the essential points is the labelling or the advertising of a remedy as a remedy.
For a specific disease?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Yes. These remedies
can be admitted into Canada or they can be manufactured in this country and can be sold by druggists on the prescription of a medical man.
Only?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Let us take, say, the remedy for epilepsy. If that is being imported or is being sold without the label anyone may buy it, but it must not be sold labelled as a remedy for epilepsy, nor may anyone advertise it as a remedy for epilepsy. It can be obtained through physicians or it can be bought provided the label does not signify that it is a remedy or treatment for epilepsy.

Suppose I go into a drug store and say to the druggist, "I am suffering from a certain attack and I want such and such a remedy for it." I name the remedy and the bottle does not contain a label. Can I get it if I name it to the druggist?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If you name the remedy itself?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Without the label?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Certainly, unless it contains a lot of narcotics.

I understand that. Here is another question. Suppose a person is suffering from rupture, and without any recommendation from a doctor or any prescription he goes to a drug store to purchase a belt or whatever the necessary appliance may be. Is there anything in the act to prevent him from doing so?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Nothing whatever. I may point out to the hon. gentleman that this does not deal with any appliance at all. One can scarcely credit it, but from time to time advertisements appear claiming a remedy for rupture; that is to say, there is a certain ointment or something that is rubbed over the area, and that is the treatment.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. R. W. GRAY (West Lambton) moved the second reading of Bill No. 100, respecting the St. Clair Transit Company.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
St. Clair Transit Company

In view of the fact that this is not a new bill but is merely an amendment to one section of an existing act, and in view of the lateness of the session, I move:
That standing order No. 104 be suspended and that the Speaker do now leave the chair in order that the house may now consider in committee of the whole Bill No. 100, an act respecting the St. Clair Transit Company.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: That motion can be made only by consent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think I can consent. My understanding is that this ought to go to the standing orders committee.
It has been there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I know, but under standing order 101:
No motion for the suspension of the standing orders or any rule respecting a petition for a private bill will be entertained, unless the same has been reported upon by the committee on standing orders, and the committee in its report shall state the grounds for recommending such suspension.
I do not want to delay the measure, but I think the course proposed would be irregular. This bill I believe raises the question of an international tunnel or bridge.
The extension of the charter of an international bridge. It has been fully discussed with the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The committee has plenty of time to consider this in the ordinary way.
No, because under standing order 105 a week's posting is required if I do not get consent to consider it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. member briDg his motion u,p on Monday when the Prime Minister is here?
I would much prefer to move the suspension of rule 105, so that the bill might be considered forthwith by the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then the hon. member will have to give notice. I cannot agree to it; I would if I could, but I cannot.
It could be referred to the private bills committee; I could move the suspension of standing order 105 so that it would not require a week's posting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to its going to the private bills committee in the most expeditious manner possible.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 70, to amend the Food and Drugs Act-Mr. MacLaren-Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 1-Regulations by governor in council.
May I ask again that the minister let this clause stand until such time as the whole of the act can be reconsidered.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member asks that the first section stand?

I simply repeat the suggestion I made this afternoon, that in view of the tremendously large powers that are being sought, an opportunity ought to be given to those interested in this matter to appear so that the whole matter may be discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am not prepared to do that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Limitations upon recommendations for self-treatment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It will now be in order to move the amendment I spoke of.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will move it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment reads:
That clause 2 be amended by adding thereto the following as section 6a:
No person or company shall import, offer for sale or sell any remedy represented by label or by advertisement to the general public as a treatment for any of the diseases, disorders or abnormal physical states named or included in schedule A to this act, or in any amendment to such schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I might explain again that this amendment to the amendment meets some objections that have been made. It gives more liberty, is less restrictive. It enables these remedies to be sold on the prescription of medical men. It enables them to be sold provided there is no label specifying that it is a remedy for any of these

Food and Drugs Act
diseases set forth in schedule A. I know it meets with less objection from some than the previous amendment.

I think the minister is making a mistake. Is it not that the amendment he proposes is a substitution for paragraph 6A of section 2? The motion should be "that paragraph 6A be deleted and the following substituted therefor."

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Quite so; that is the amendment.
That is not what is being done.

It seems to me the
present section should be struck out and the amendment substituted for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Quite so. The motion is that section 6A mentioned in the bill be struck out and the amendment substituted for it.

No, you are striking out
section 2.
The intention is to amend 6A of section 2. You delete section 2 entirely and put in this new section.
Shall that carry?
What is the substitution?

If I understand the matter aright we objected to this section 6A when it was before us the other day. We objected to the words "manufacture," "advertise," and so on, and in the amendment those words have been deleted. Otherwise the paragraph is very much as it was before.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is not my interpretation of it. For instance, now it is simply restricted to the sale to the general public. As I understand it the motion is to strike out the addition to the act, section 6A as originally printed in the bill, and substitute the proposed section.
Section 6A is not a section of the bill.

All I have before me is:
2. The said act is further amended by adding thereto the following section immediately after section 6 thereof:
Then the amendment proposes the new section 6A:
Would you mind reading the proposed new section again?

The amendment reads:
No person or company shall import, offer for sale or sell any remedy represented by label or by advertisement to the general public as a treatment for any of the diseases, disorders or abnormal physical states named or included in schedule A to this act or in any amendment to such schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think the matter is quite clear. My motion is to insert a new section in the act. It is to be inserted between sections 6 and 7, and we are naming it section 6A. Nothing is to be stricken out; it is simply the addition of a new section to the act.
If the chairman would just add to what he has read the words "that section 2 be amended by striking out paragraph 6A thereof and substituting therefor the following," we would have the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
right. So far as the original act is concerned it merely adds a new subsection.
Shall the amendment carry?

No. The amendment
now reads:
No person or company shall import, offer for sale or sell any remedy represented by label or by advertisement to the general public as a treatment for any of the diseases-
And so on. I submit that under the Interpretation Act the words "or company" are superfluous. The amendment should read, "no person shall import" and so on. We want to get at the meaning of this amendment. I take it that bottle must have on it some kind of label. There is nothing in the definition of the Interpretation Act about what a label is. We do not know whether the label must be on the bottle, on the carton or inside the carton quite apart from the bottle itself "-represented by label or by advertisement to the general public." Does that mean that no person or company shall import, offer for sale or sell any remedy represented by a label to the general public, or does it mean that no person or company shall import, offer for sale or sell any remedy to the general public? Apparently that means that on that label there must be no representation or advertisement to the general public. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
No, it is limited to remedies for those diseases or conditions specified in the schedule.
Food and Drugs Act

Quite so, but on those remedies that affect any of the abnormal physical states mentioned in the schedule there must be no label or representation or advertisement to the general public. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Not representing it as being a remedy or treatment for the diseases specified in the schedule.

Or by advertisement to the general public. What is an advertisement to the general public? I understand that the intention, though it is not expressly stated, is to limit the advertising of remedies used for these specific cases to the medical profession. If that be so where does the general public start and where does it end? How are you going to determine what is an advertisement to the general public? Apparently I cannot advertise in the daily newspapers any remedy that may be used as a treatment for the abnormal physical states mentioned in the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Of course you can, if you are addressing it to the medical profession.

I gathered that that was the intention, but what is said in this house in the discussion of the bill as to what the intention of the minister may be cannot be used as evidence before the courts. I have to have a clear expression of what the intention and effect of the law may be, so that when I appear in a court the judge, or the person charged with the interpretation of the statute, will know exactly what it means or will have some means of ascertaining the fundamental intention. The minister has said what he means, but the amendment is not clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It is stated in the
amendment.
Read the amendment from the first.

The amendment reads:
No person or company shall import, offer for sale or sell any remedy represented by label or by advertisement to the general public as a treatment ...
And so on. Now, that is all right, but there is no definition as to what "the general public" may mean. The minister says that I may advertise it to the medical profession, but the amendment does not so indicate. I can advertise to the medical profession in various ways. I understand the minister to mean that I may take to a daily paper in Ottawa an advertisement for one of these remedies advertised as a treatment for some abnormal

physical state and have such advertisement inserted so that I would be advertising to the general public remedies for all of these abnormal physical states, provided that I put at the top, underneath or at the corner of the advertisement the words "This advertisement is directed to the medical profession only." I understand that that is the intention. I understand further that I may advertise in a so-called or genuine medical review which may be directed, as is usually the case, to the medical profession. I may advertise in the Lancet, the English periodical devoted almost exclusively to the medical profession, any of the remedies to be used as a treatment for any one of the abnormal physical states mentioned in the schedule. My own impression is that if I were to advertise in a dental or pharmaceutical review I would not be advertising to the general public. But where is the line to be drawn? What is the determining line? I cannot advertise in the daily press without the insertion of some restrictive words, but if I can advertise in a medical review, then what is a medical review? I have before me one of these reviews; I shall not mention the name of it, but in it appears an advertisement of a uric acid eliminator, a well known French product, and such specific ailments are mentioned, as gout, lithiasis, neuralgia, rheumatism, arteriosclerosis and obesity. If the bill and schedule become law in their present form, in view of the fact that this publication is not an ordinary review but is directed to the general public, the manufacturers of the product in question will have to eliminate the words "arterioolerosis and obesity." Although this remedy is not one used exclusively for these ailments, yet it is a solvent used in a case of arteriosclerosis as a uric acid eliminator and in a case of obesity as another sort of eliminator. I ask the minister this:	If I put
in the advertisement the words, "This advertisement is directed to the medical profession only," may it circulate among the general public as an advertisement for arteriosclerosis and obesity?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
If it is directed to the
medical profession, yes.
But I want to find out when it is directed to the medical profession and when it is not directed to the medical profession.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The answer is, when
it says so-that is all.

It would have been
much better if the statute had been made clear. But if the minister states that tomorrow I may go to one of the daily papers

Food and Drugs Act
and advertise a remedy for the treatment of one or all of the ailments mentioned in the schedule, and I can do that simply by putting a line at the top of or underneath the advertisement saying, " This is directed exclusively to the medical profession " that arrangement may be all right, but I suggest it is not a proper way to do business.
Where will you sell your product?

That is why I say there is no reason for the inclusion in the schedule of quite a large number of these so-called abnormal physical conditions. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden), differing from other opinions which have been expressed, says that a certain number of these ailments are not abnormal physical states. They should be excluded. The difficulty is that one cannot advertise to the general public any one of these remedies as a treatment for the abnormal physical states mentioned in the schedule. But I want to know where I can do it. I believe I have made myself clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Wherever you consider
it to your advantage, that is the answer. There are medical journals without number, and there are periodicals and, if you wish, the press. This amendment is intended not to be extreme but to be a moderate measure, and not to go too far in advance of general opinion. Therefore an advertisement to the profession is allowed or allowable in any form you wish.

I intimated to the committee this afternoon that I thought this legislation was to a great extent farcical. Many forms of disease are mentioned for which no one would think of advertising cures before the general public. So far as those forms of disease are concerned, I believe we may put them out of our minds; we do not need to go over them again. In the case of quite a number, however, there is potential danger in druggists or proprietary people advertising remedies. All these particular forms of disease I have in mind certainly require the attention of a skilled physician. However, to my mind the whole discussion circles around the one disease which I discussed at length this afternoon and in connection with which we as medical men have had but scant success in the matter of treatment. The amendment states:
No person or company shall import, offer for sale or sell any remedy represented by label or by advertisement to the general public ...
And so on. We know of one firm at least which has been successful in treating by mail a malady in the treatment of which medical men have had very little or no success. A number of people throughout the dominion are suffering from that disease, and at the present time they are apprehensive that this legislation will remove from them the possibility of obtaining the medicine for the relief of their condition. The amendment plainly says that this medicine shall not be advertised to the public. How then shall other victims who will suffer from this disease in the future be relieved, or how will they be informed of the fact that there is a remedy that can relieve them? If the remedy cannot be advertised I do not see how they can learn about it.

Get a good
medical man.
It is true that there are a lot of good medical men, but there are a few conditions that medical men have not been able to control entirely, and this is one of them.
Do you want the sufferers to go to quacks?
I have no interest whatever in any quack company or quack doctor, but if any quack doctor is able to give relief for a condition where I cannot give relief, I say more power to him.
Have you ever met one who could?

I have met many cases,
and for that reason I say without hesitation that if this legislation is enforced it will be positively unfair to a number of epileptics in this dominion. I have no personal interest in any epileptic but I like to see people in any such condition treated fairly and given a chance; for it is well known that if the disease is allowed to run on for a number of years without relief it affects the mind and the sufferer becomes feebleminded.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I had intended to wait until we reached the schedule before saying anything with reference to any of the diseases listed, but I feel I should not delay, and that I should say something about epilepsy.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have had communications and reports on different diseases, and recently I have received from members of parliament and others a considerable number of letters with reference to the administration

[DOT]1030
Food and Drugs Act

of a certain remedy for epilepsy. So far as I can tell, and I think this applies to all of them, they originated at the request of a medical firm in Chicago, the Western Medical Corporation. I should like to read this communication to the house. It is a letter on the heading of the Western Medical Corporation, and the directing physician is Harry L. James, MU. The letter is dated May 25, 1934, and this particular letter is addressed to a lady. It reads:
Dear Miss,-
Do you know that a new Canadian law has been proposed to make it impossible for you to obtain treatment for epilepsy attacks except through a physician? This means that you could not buy medicines from any concern in the United States or in Canada for epilepsy attacks.
I think that is correct so far as it goes. It is correct if it were labelled; it is not correct if there were no labels on it. The letter continues:
This matter was brought to our attention by one of our Canadian customers who was greatly disturbed at the possibility of not being able to obtain our medicines should the bill be passed. We refer to the bill sponsored by the Hon. Doctor Murray MacLaren, Minister of Pensions and National Health, now in its second reading.
It occurred to me that all of our Canadian patients might not be aware of this impending legislation. Therefore I suggest that if you feel the passage of this bill might seriously affect you because you could no longer obtain medicines from us, it would no doubt be a good plan to write to your representative in the dominion House of Commons

That has been duly done.
-asking that the disease epilepsy be removed from the list. You might also add that you consider it a grave injustice to be forced to go to a local physician for treatment.
Immediate action is no doubt necessary if you are to cause the removal of the disease epilepsy from the list of diseases contained in the bill.
Will you let us hear from you as to what answer your representative gives you?
Sincerely,
Harry L. James, M.D.,
Directing Physician.

What is
the name of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The Western Medical
Corporation. So far as I am aware, all the letters and copies of letters that have reached me or the department have been sent on the invitation of the Western Medical Corporation through their directing physician.
I never got one.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It was not necessary
in my hon. friend's case.
I am not suffering from epilepsy.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
There, Mr. Chairman,
you have the fons et origo of all this trouble about epilepsy; and the corporation makes its appeal attractive by the distribution of a three dollar coupon to all those who are buying these medicines
I would like to say, for this is rather important, that the formula is on these bottles when they are sold under the act. The remedy is luminal, and for many cases of epilepsy that is probably the most suitable and effective remedy, but I saw a letter not long ago in which the correspondent said he had been taking luminal and it was not useful, and that he got the medicine of this company and it was just the thing. The ordinary trade term for this remedy is luminal, but there are at least two other long scientific names, and if they are used, naturally the general public are not aware that it is luminal they are taking, and yet it is the same thing. The remedy I say is luminal, and it is quite a good remedy as a palliative in epilepsy. But epilepsy is due to different causes. I grant you that in many cases it is idiopathic, that there is no discernible cause for it, but in other cases that is not so. It may be due to arterial degeneration, or to luetic infection, or to injuries. Strangely enough I have a letter before me from a woman who writes that she had received a fractured skull from a kick by a horse, and she was taking this remedy for epilepsy. That was essentially a case for examination by a surgeon or physician, not a case for treatment by correspondence with a doctor a thousand miles away.
She might have had Jacksonian epilepsy and had the epilepsy as a result of the kick on the head.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I cannot say as to that. I am giving her statement, that she had epilepsy, that she had a fracture of the skull caused 'by a kick from a horse. There is no mystery about these things, and I believe many of them would be wise if they took the same thing. They can go to a druggist and get it themselves if they desire without there being any advertising or anything else. This matter has been brought to the attention of the public in this way. I do not know that one can blame him for following his business instincts, but our Object is to try to protect the public and see that they do not incessantly and continually take something which they may not need. I agree that a cure for epilepsy is not known but sometimes it dis-

Food and Drugs Act
appears although in other cases it becomes worse. I think all cases should receive skilled attention. AH we are saying is that these things shall not bear labels and be advertised. To that small extent we are trying to protect the public.

Would the minister be kind enough to answer one question for me? He stated a moment ago that as long as a product was not labelled for the cure of a disease it could be sold to the general public in any drug store.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Absolutely.

Could a man sell a drug advertised in a manner similar to the letter which the minister read provided the bottle was not labelled? 'Is there anything in the proposed amendment which would prevent a manufacturer from sending out circular letters of the kind which the minister read, provided he does not label his bottle as a remedy for a disease listed in schedule A? This is what the druggist wants to know. I have received sheaves of telegrams from pharmaceutical associations all the way from Toronto down to Quebec asking me to ascertain if there is anything in the present law or in the proposed amendment which would prevent a druggist or a pharmacist or a manufacturer from advertising a product so long as he does not label the bottle. That is the first point. Second, is there anything in the law or in the amendment which prevents a manufacturer or a druggist from advertising a product as long as the advertising or the sample bottle is addressed direct to the medical profession? If the minister can clear up those points, I shall be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My answer to the first and third questions is that it would be allowable under the act. As to the question whether or not a druggist could advertise, I should like to know what it is he wishes to advertise. He must have something to advertise.
Suppose it is advertising a product to cure epilepsy.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He could not do that.
But he could do that to the medical profession?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Absolutely.
How could he do that to the medical profession, in a medical review or in a newspaper?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
In both.
74726-255 J

He could do that in a newspaper provided he labelled his bottles in some way. I should like to get the proper phraseology in order that there may be no misunderstanding when I advise a client. What phraseology must the advertiser or the manufacturer of a product use in order to protect himself when he is advertising in a daily newspaper?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He could do it, but you are speaking about something that is not done.
There has been no need to do it up to the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It is not done. All these things appear in medical journals, but I grant you it could be donej That is not the way to do it and that is not the way it is done. He could address it to the medical profession and say:	This is the remedy that Doctor
James prescribes for epilepsy.

Let me get this thing right for my own personal information. Here is an advertisement. Under the term of this amendment it could not appear in a daily newspaper because it refers to arteriosclerosis and obesity, and those diseases are referred to in this schedule. Will the minister tell me what phraseology I could use for this advertisement in order to put this product before the general public and advertise it as it is being advertised in this magazine?
Head it "for the medical profession only."
I am asking the minister, and I think he can answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The minister will answer with great pleasure. What is the name of the product the hon. member is speaking of?
This is an advertisement for urodonal. It states that it is a uric acid eliminator. Then it goes on to say what it is good for, and among other things it mentions arteriosclerosis and obesity.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: State that it is for the medical profession.
All I have to do is label it to the medical profession and then the officers of the department would not prosecute?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is right.

In order to relieve my anxiety I should like the minister to confirm one statement. Should an individual
Food and Drugs Act

advertise, either in a publication or by private letter or even on a bottle label, if that was addressed to the medical profession would he be interfered with by this amendment or by the present act?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It would not touch that.

I received a letter from a person in my constituency which is somewhat along the lines of the letter read by the minister. It states that one of the family is afflicted with epilepsy and had been unable to obtain any relief except through the remedy prepared by Doctor James of Chicago. These people were protesting strongly against the passage of this amendment. As I understand the amendment, it will mean that anyone troubled with epilepsy must secure this remedy through a prescription by a medical man. I should like to know if a person could import this remedy from Doctor James so long as it came in without a label?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Certainly.
Supposing it did come in without a label, what would the customs department do? Would they allow it to come in?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Certainly. The difficulty has been in tracing these things once they got into the country, but an individual could order through the customs provided the label did not state it was a remedy for epilepsy. Of course the ingredients would have to be mentioned on the label.

I was very glad to hear
the minister state quite definitely a few minutes ago that luminal is what this Doctor James of Chicago is sending to his patients. Luminal is a well known hypnotic and we medical men have been using it for -ten or twelve years. Phenobarbital and luminal and a number of other allied products have exactly the same effect upon the human economy. I cannot state definitely that I have ever prescribed luminal for epilepsy but I should think that the medical profession at large has been in the habit of trying all these sedatives and hypnotics in an endeavour to control the malady. This afternoon I had on my desk four letters from different parts of Canada-and hon. members intimated at the time that many of them had also received these letters-in which the writers stated quite definitely that after treating with medical men for a considerable time without any result whatever they had obtained relief from attacks of epilepsy. If relief has been given

through the use of the drug luminal then it is a mighty good thing for us to know, and perhaps Doctor James will lose his business forthwith. But in the event of luminal not giving the desired results, I should certainly hope that this Health department of the dominion would not put it beyond the power of people to obtain the remedy that has brought them relief in the past. I have no other interest in it in the world; I am a medical man and I like to see disease relieved where possible, so that I have no other interest except the relief of sufferers from epilepsy. The minister stated a moment ago that this remedy could be brought in if the label were removed. That I suggest is a roundabout way of getting the remedy to a sick person, but still it is better than no way at all, and if it is possible for these epileptics to obtain whatever will relieve them from their malady, provided the label is removed, that satisfies me for the time being.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 3-Sale, etc., of compound vinegar, etc., prohibited.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The difficulty of distinguishing on the one hand between cider vinegar and vinegar derived from wine and, on the other, acetic acid which may be obtained by distillation of wood and other materials is considerable; hence in different manufactures such as pickles if the synthetic vinegar is used it is very difficult to detect it from the proper domestic vinegar, and this section affords protection, so that people will be assured that they are obtaining cider vinegar. That is the object of the amendment; it is not allowed to be on the premises of manufacturers.

On schedule A.

There are a few of these abnormal physical states which in my opinion should not be in the schedule. I fully appreciate, as I have told the minister repeatedly, the fact that in a number of instances people ought to be protected against themselves, and the vast majority of the physical states mentioned in the schedule should remain, I think. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) this afternoon reviewed them, and though I have not the competency to review them all I know some of them. Take arteriosclerosis, for instance. Everyone knows that that is hardening of the arteries, and once they have started to harden there is no cure.

Food and Drugs Act
But certain solvents may be used which will give considerable relief and restore to the arteries a certain degree of elasticity. The minister has said that certain remedies which heretofore could be used only as specifics might, by some side issue, be used for some of these physical states, and that clears up the situation to some extent. I must repeat however that the word "influenza" should be struck out. Ordinary people do not regard grippe and colds as influenza, although many of those who are dealing in matters of this kind like to give these maladies high sounding names; and unless they are advertised to the medical profession, then these remedies may not be advertised. I think another one that ought to come out is the supposed abnormal physical state of obesity. I quite realize there are two kinds. I know that in certain instances people have been led to believe that a certain quack medicine would bring them back to a sort of normal state, but owing to the peculiar cause of corpulency or obesity due to the deficiency of the thyroid gland medical treatment is absolutely necessary; the so-called eliminators would be useful but would aggravate the condition. But inasmuch as there are two kinds of remedies, one based on thyroid extracts and the other based on diet, the distinction should be made so as to enable those who sell certain laxatives and salts to advertise them as a relief for that type of obesity, which does not result upon thyroid or pituitary deficiency and the like. I should like to see the word "obesity" taken out; at any rate it ought to be qualified in some way. If the minister would confine it to obesity that comes within the endogenous class, namely, where there is thyroid deficiency, I would agree with that; but in the other kind, usually called exogenous obesity, which simply results from autointoxication, bad food or bad elimination, the remedies in this class ought to be allowed. If the minister would qualify in some way the word "obesity" then I should be in perfect accord with the bill and I should say he ought to be commended for having to that extent improved the conditions under which the national health of Canada is maintained.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I should like to meet the wishes of my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Chevirier) but I do not see how I can. There are more than two varieties of obesity; there are four or five anyway. The hon. member has referred to thyroid deficiency, but there are forms due to other defective glands in the system. And further, as to the remedies that are used for obesity, the thyroid perhaps we will agree has to be used with considerable
discretion, but there is another that occurs to me, that is what is called nitro compound. It has produced unfortunate results, so much so that its use is not permitted in certain countries. Obesity in elderly people is rather a formidable condition. If one is relying on the exclusion of thyroid and nitro compound and using aperients or laxatives in moderation I am afraid it is something that will soothe them but will do them no good. I think it is proper that the name should be retained.

The explanatory note states that the purpose of this bill is to bring these two acts into conformity, and that under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act certain remedies may not be sold. I should like to ask whether in the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act there is the same proviso regarding importation. We are providing here that no person or company shall import, but in looking over the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act I could see no provision regarding importation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No; that is taken care of by departmental regulation under the act. The list is the same in both acts.

I should like to urge upon the minister and the department that they enforce the strictest possible measures against the sale by druggists and quacks of measures for the condition last named on the list. It is much more seriously fraught with danger than any of the other diseases mentioned, so far as I can see. The strictest possible means of enforcement should be employed to control promiscuous prescribing for this condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I shall make a note of that. As far as advertising is concerned, which is the principal danger, it is being carefully watched.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 53, to amend the Canada Grain Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Stirling in the chair.
On section 1-Tentative standard samples of western grain.

As I have a few remarks to make perhaps I may as well make them at this stage. When the committee on agriculture and colonization completed its labours a statement was apparently given to the press indicating that the decision arrived at had been unanimous. That is not quite correct. I know I was agreeable to doing almost anything for the present in the way of getting rid of this question that would improve the situation and improve the bill that the minister had introduced. It had been a source of controversy at home and abroad for the last four years or more. The alternative to doing what we did was to keep up the controversy, and that did not seem to be advisable or in anyone's interest, particularly the interest of the wheat growers of the west. To that extent I was agreeable to the amendments made to the amended bill. The controversy that I refer to was carried on by a number of gentlemen who I think should have known a lot better. One of them was Mr. Short, president of the Canadian Millers' Association, and the other two were Doctor Tory and Doctor Newton. The first remark I would make with regard to the evidence and to the change in the amended bill is that the minister did not carry out the recommendations of his board of grain commissioners in bringing the bill before the house at all, because we find on page 6 of the last report of the board of grain commissioners that the following report was made to the minister by the board on the 8th of January, 1934:
Amendments to the Canada Grain Act
The board has continued to investigate the effect of allowing garnet wheat to be placed in No. 2 Manitoba northern wheat. We are substantially in agreement that garnet wheat should be given an independent classification,

but in view of the present low price of wheat and the difficulties of the wheat producer, we are of the opinion that it might not be advisable to proceed with changes in the classification at the present session.
That is a very concise and understandable recommendation, but the minister proceeded to disobey it and to introduce the amendments to the Canada Grain Act now before us. It was not made apparent at any of the meetings of the committee by any of the witnesses as to just why the minister departed from the recommendations of his advisers, the board of grain commissioners, who are recognized not only as capable but very honourable men who have the whole grain trade at their finger tips. An attempt was made to some extent by the two gentlemen themselves to show why they had changed their minds, though they did not exactly say they had done so. The evidence they produced to warrant a change, however, was very slim indeed.
If the minister was not governed by the advice of the board-as certainly he was not- on whose advice did he act, I wonder? In the Montreal Gazette of March 6 I find an interview given by Mr. Short, the gentleman to whom I have referred. I believe he is reported too fully for me to read the whole interview, but apparently he took a flying trip to Vancouver before he went to Montreal. I have no doubt he went there on business, but so far as the public were concerned his chief business was to carry on propaganda against garnet wheat. I believe we had one complaint about garnet wheat from Vancouver, from the harbour board or someone in that vicinity. Then, as Mr. Short travelled eastward via Calgary, on the Canadian Pacific railway, further convenient and illuminating interviews were given, all derogatory to garnet wheat. He represented the poor downtrodden wheat growers of the south as carrying the northern growers on their backs. As he came on to Regina he emitted more of these interviews, equally damaging to garnet wheat and equally straining the truth and drawing a mighty long bow. He reached Winnipeg and there were more interviews, and I have before me his final peroration on the dangers of garnet wheat:
The over-all average quality of Canadian wheat is materially reduced by the lower grades from the northern areas, which primarily result from the variety of lesser quality and earlier ripening wheats sown, noteably garnet.
A recent article by James McLeash in the Winnipeg Free Press, said Mr. Short, sounds a timely note of warning to Canada in pointing out the steadily developing aggressive agricultural policy of the Argentinian government.

Canada Grain Act
The Argentine government clearly foresees the imperative need of quality standard as a prime essential to successful wheat marketing in the future, and is bending every effort to raise the standard of the crop by the elimination of various varieties of wheat which affect adversely the general average standard.
"There is no doubt," he continued, "that the method of grading in Canada in the recent years, which has developed through the varieties of lesser quality wheats grown, notably the northern areas, has reduced materially the margin of superiority which characterized Canadian wheat compared with other wheats.
Incidentally I may say that is not correct.
Unless some steps are taken to prevent the steady deterioration in the average quality of our crop, our own situation taken in conjunction with that of other countries such as the Argentine, which is improving the quality of its crop, will naturally result in narrowing the margin of superiority of the Canadian crop over its competition to an uncomfortable minimum.
That is not correct, either. I would not like to say how many miles it is from being correct.
It is surely axiomatic that a price premium can be maintained only in strict relation to quality superiority. It is well within the realms of probability that the slow movement of this year's crop in no small measure involves the question of relative quality in respect to relative price. It is a fact that at the present time there are several millions of No. 2 northern wheat at the Pacific coast for which it is extremely difficult to find buyers because of the heavy admixture of the inferior northern grades.
There was no such evidence as that given; the contrary was the case. There was no congestion of No. 2 that could not find buyers. One gentleman said there was, but two or three others challenged the statement.
A definite and aggressive wheat policy is urgently needed, not as a party platform and, in consequence, a political football, but as a national program.
The light is not as good for reading as I would like to have it, but Mr. Short continues on that line, getting worse as he goes on. That interview was given on March 6 and the bill was placed on the order paper on April 9 or 10, just long enough afterwards for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) to have the thought put into his mind by Mr. Short expressed in the form of a bill. The fact that these two events occurred so closely to each other is not proof positive that one was the cause of the other, but at all events we have seen that the minister has not followed the advice of his advisers, his own board of grain commissioners, while he had an opportunity at least of following this other advice. I do not know whether there was some
additional advice from some other source than Mr. Short; all I do know is that the minister did not follow the advice of his very competent board of grain commissioners.
Well, I do not know what they are there for unless it is for that purpose. When that board was appointed in 1929 we thought our problems were over with regard to the Grain Act; we thought we would not need any more commissions, because we had a competent board of practical men who would be able to keep the ministry, whoever they were, in pretty close touch with the requirements of the country in this important respect. I have one or two notes before me. They are not very long, but I should like to point out that we have made the change in the amended act to mean that it was not to go to the standards board to be bandied about a third time by that institution, but that the government was to take the responsibility as they are now doing of grading garnet wheat along the line of statutory grades, and giving it the same status as the other statutory grades, namely No. 1 northern and No. 2 northern. There is a vast difference between that procedure and sending it back once more to the standards board, a body which had already tried the case and adjudicated upon it, once ex parte and a second time with Doctor Newman in attendance to tell his side of the story. The minister had the remarkable audacity after those two experiences to ask this House of Commons to refer this knotty question back a third time to the standards board, thereby escaping the responsibility himself of making the change. The committee thought otherwise, and this amended bill is the result. But in order to avoid further propaganda by these experts in the propaganda and plagiaristic line to whom I have referred-I have named the three gentlemen- I do not know what assurances we are going to have that as soon as this bill has passed further propaganda will not be set up by Mr. Short and others to drive garnet out of No. 3 northern. According to the recommendation of the committee there will be No. 1 C.W. garnet, No. 2 C.W. garnet, and the lower grades will come in their respective regular grades. There is nothing to hinder Mr. Short from waking up some morning with the determination to drive garnet off the map and out of the country, and to start up another hallabaloo. He knows how to do it. I feel like taking my hat off to any person who does a thing well, even if I do not approve of it. I must say I have never seen a more successful propagandist than
Canada Grain Act

Mr. Short, unless it be Doctor Tory and his satellite colleague, the other gentleman to whom I referred.
So it would seem that we are not altogether out of the woods, unless the minister can do something with two of these gentlemen who are officials of his and servants of the crown. In many respects they are very good servants but they have a mania for promotion, propaganda and limelight. I suppose that is a prevalent disease. It seems to me that sometimes it is quite contagious, and we have to take great care lest we contract it ourselves. I will say this, that if the action of the government and of the committee results in driving garnet out of the country-and I anticipate it will; I have never had any illusions about that-then a great wrong will have been done our prairie northern hinterlands and its people. No wheat has yet been found which was graded outside of the regular Manitoba grades and lived more than three or four years afterwards. That is a serious contemplation. One gentleman has been knighted-I refer to Sir Charles Saunders- for establishing and setting up garnet along with three other varieties of wheat. Is someone going to qualify for knighthood by killing it?

There is a continuity about all this cereal research work ever since the late Doctor William Saunders came to Canada. He was the originator of all this breeding and development of Canadian wheat, and the real one, too. He has done a great work for Canada. At any rate, the minister should not feel snuffy about it because it may be that if he succeeds in killing this wheat which Sir Charles established or, at least, had something to do with, then there will be possibly one person knighted for establishing it and another, possibly the minister or Mr. Short, knighted for killing it. That seems to be contradictory.
I would suggest to the minister that he should bring this whole question of the recent conflict between the staff of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce to the attention of the cabinet. That was the chief reason which actuated the efforts and decision of the committee, namely to put a stop to the everlasting bickering between the officers of those departments, not to mention their respective ministers, to the discredit of the government and the discredit of us all. They are all good men, but what can we expect when we have a hydra-headed department of agriculture presided over by two ministers? You cannot expect anything else; so long as there are two capable and strong minded men you are bound to have not only friction between them but friction between their respective staffs. If the government wish to follow up some of their reforms, and especially the reforms in connection with price spreads, mass buying and business ethics, they might very well consider the ethics of the departments of Agriculture and Trade and Commerce, and the conflict going on between those departments, one which has not been engendered by themselves alone, because it is a legacy handed down for the last thirty years. As a matter of fact, for the last fifty years the Department of Agriculture has been presided over by two heads. For thirty years it has been controlled by the ministers of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce, and for the preceding twenty years the Minister of Inland Revenue had a hand in it. As a matter of fact, it was the Minister of Inland Revenue who in the first instance introduced and sponsored the Grain Act in the House of Commons. That was the department which had to do with tobacco, whisky

Canada Grain Act
and so on. So that in Ottawa for many years the Department of Agriculture was just a minus factor in this respect in this social and political centre of Ottawa, and that is where it stayed during all those years. I believe, Mr. Chairman, if we are to cure the present difficulty and avoid similar difficulties in the future, the sooner we get all of agriculture under the Minister of Agriculture, the better it will be. I do not know of any country in the world, and particularly other countries on this continent-and they would be more comparable, particularly the United States-where there are two heads to the Department of Agriculture. I will say that that condition is not the fault of the minister, and I will say further that neither he nor the Minister of Agriculture is in a position to agitate for a change, because they would be open to the charge of having created a commotion within the ranks of the cabinet. That is why, being outside of the cabinet, I take this opportunity to make the suggestion, a suggestion which I hope will not be unpleasant or unwelcome to the government.
I should be surprised if the government were not aware of the fact that this embarrassing situation should continue for as short a time as possible. Such a condition does not promote good results, but develops the opposite. We know about the flair that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has developed for agriculture. We know about his little venture in connection with the Yorkshire geldings, for instance. We hear about his other venture when he took a shot at a bunch of dairy cows, and conceived the idea that it would be a good idea to send them tcf Australia. We hear about the Per-cheron mares, and about his raising Ned all around. These are substantial reports which come to me and seem almost as authentic as the famous "Yorkshire geldings."
If the Prime Minister were here I would ask him to suppress this state of affairs in the interests of agriculture. This is not the first time that we have had bickerings and backbiting at the heads of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce. I will ask you, Mr. Chairman, if there would have been any trouble about garnet wheat if there had been only one head. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) has been opposed to these changes all along, and no wonder because about two-thirds of his constituents are garnet growers, so you can quite understand his anxiety about the matter. It is very creditable to him: for the sake of seeming harmony he and his staff decided to compose their differences with the Minister of
Trade and Commerce and his staff by adopting this bill as a substitute for the other one which the Minister of Trade and Commerce brought down. The Minister of Trade and Commerce looks half cross at me, but if he wants to say anything 'he will have lots of chances after I am through. But those are the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, under which I at all events would agree to anything almost for the present rather than have constant haggling and scrapping between the ministers, both of whom are no doubt trying to do their duty in their respective spheres, with their staffs also doing their duty in their spheres. This condition of affairs, where there is constant haggling and scrapping, should not be tolerated for one minute longer than it is necessary to change it.
I have nothing to add further if the bill is as it left the committee, and I presume it is. There is a chart here that would be very useful if the minister distributed it. I do not know, Mr. Chairman, how we are going to deal with this bill properly unless it is reprinted. This chart that I have here shows the grades, and if there are no other charts for distribution I should be glad to pass this around.
